neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented to person, place, time, and situation. Glasgow Coma Scale 15. Speech fluent with normal rate, rhythm, and prosody. No dysarthria or aphasia. Attention intact, able to spell WORLD backwards and perform serial sevens without error. Recall 3/3 objects at 5 minutes. Affect is somewhat flat but cooperative. She appears anxious and focused on her leg symptoms.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: CN II: Visual fields full to confrontation bilaterally. Pupils equal, round, reactive to light 3mm to 2mm bilaterally. Fundoscopic exam normal, no papilledema. CN III/IV/VI: Extraocular movements intact without nystagmus or diplopia. CN V: Sensation intact to light touch in all three divisions bilaterally. Masseter strength symmetric. CN VII: Face symmetric at rest and with activation. CN VIII: Hearing grossly intact to finger rub bilaterally. CN IX/X: Palate elevates symmetrically, gag reflex intact. CN XI: Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. CN XII: Tongue midline, no fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk normal throughout. Tone normal in all extremities, no spasticity or rigidity. Upper extremities: strength 5/5 bilaterally in all muscle groups (deltoids, biceps, triceps, wrist extensors, grip). Right lower extremity: give-way weakness in hip flexion, knee extension, and ankle dorsiflexion — patient initiates movement to 4/5 then suddenly gives way. Left lower extremity: 5/5 in all muscle groups. Hoover sign POSITIVE on the right — involuntary hip extension detected when testing contralateral hip flexion, contradicting apparent voluntary weakness. No pronator drift. No muscle atrophy or fasciculations.
neurological_exam.sensory: Reports decreased sensation to light touch and pinprick over the entire right leg in a non-dermatomal distribution with a sharp midline split at the groin. Vibration and proprioception intact throughout. Sensory findings do not conform to any peripheral nerve, root, or spinal cord pattern.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally, triceps 2+ bilaterally, brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally, patellar 2+ bilaterally, Achilles 2+ bilaterally. Plantar responses are flexor (downgoing) bilaterally. Reflexes are symmetric and normal, inconsistent with upper or lower motor neuron lesion.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose testing normal bilaterally without dysmetria. Heel-to-shin testing normal on the left. On the right, patient demonstrates inconsistent performance with moments of normal coordination interspersed with apparent difficulty. No intention tremor. Rapid alternating movements intact bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Patient initially states she cannot walk. When assisted to standing, demonstrates a dragging gait of the right leg with inconsistent pattern. When distracted by conversation, leg movements briefly normalize. No Trendelenburg sign. Tandem gait not attempted due to patient's reported inability. Romberg testing: dramatic swaying without falling, with ability to self-correct. Overall gait pattern is non-physiologic.
neurological_exam.additional: During the examination, the patient had a witnessed episode of bilateral upper and lower extremity shaking lasting approximately 90 seconds. Eyes were noted to be forcefully closed during the event. The shaking was arrhythmic, waxing and waning, with side-to-side head movements. She remained responsive to voice during portions of the event. No post-ictal confusion, no cyanosis, no tongue biting, no incontinence. The episode self-resolved with verbal reassurance. This is consistent with a psychogenic non-epileptic seizure (PNES). Video-EEG was being recorded during this event.

patient.chief_complaint: Right leg weakness and episodes of shaking spells for 4 weeks
patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Lauren Hadley is a 28-year-old right-handed woman who presents to the neurology inpatient service with a four-week history of progressive right leg weakness and recurrent episodes of whole-body shaking. The symptoms began approximately four weeks ago when she noticed her right leg 'giving out' while walking up stairs at work. Over the following week the weakness progressed to the point where she had difficulty walking without a limp, and she has been using a cane for the past two weeks. She reports the leg feels 'dead' and she cannot control it. She also describes decreased sensation over the entire right leg, stating it feels numb from the hip down. Concurrently, she began experiencing episodes of shaking approximately three weeks ago. These episodes involve bilateral arm and leg trembling, sometimes with her eyes rolling back. They last between one and three minutes. During some episodes she reports being able to hear people around her but is unable to respond. There is no tongue biting, urinary incontinence, or post-ictal confusion. The episodes occur one to two times per day and seem to be triggered by emotional stress or fatigue. She was seen at an outside emergency department two weeks ago where a CT head was normal and she was referred for outpatient neurology follow-up, but her symptoms worsened and she was admitted for further evaluation including video-EEG monitoring. She reports significant psychosocial stress including workplace conflict with a new supervisor, her partner's recent unemployment, and a minor motor vehicle accident six weeks ago that she found very distressing despite no physical injury. She denies any prior history of seizures, stroke, or neurological disease. She has been taking sertraline for anxiety and depression. She is very concerned she may have multiple sclerosis or a brain tumor and has been researching her symptoms extensively online.

output.summary: Functional neurological disorder is characterized by positive clinical signs of internal inconsistency — Hoover sign, give-way weakness, and absence of ictal EEG correlate during captured events. The CODES RCT demonstrated CBT reduces dissociative seizure frequency compared with standard care. Specialized physiotherapy using distraction-based movement retraining shows benefit for functional motor symptoms in observational cohorts. Earlier diagnosis is associated with better outcomes in longitudinal studies. Antidepressants address comorbid mood and anxiety disorders but have limited direct evidence for core functional symptoms.

differential.key_features: Witnessed convulsive-appearing events; ictal video-EEG showing absence of electrographic correlate during a captured habitual event is the key differentiator.
Sensorimotor symptoms in a young adult raise demyelinating disease; brain (and when indicated spine) MRI without T2/FLAIR lesions or enhancement argues against an active demyelinating process.
Sudden focal deficit raises stroke; non-anatomical weakness pattern with positive Hoover sign, normal MRI/DWI, and intact reflexes argue against vascular etiology.
Focal complaints warrant imaging; normal brain MRI without lesion, mass, or enhancement effectively excludes a structural cause for the presenting deficit.
Non-dermatomal sensory loss, normal reflexes, and (when obtained) normal EMG/NCS argue against peripheral nerve or root pathology.
Episodic neurological symptoms can occur in autoimmune encephalitis; normal MRI, normal EEG background, and (when obtained) negative antibody panel render this very unlikely.

optimal_actions.action: Elicit positive rule-in signs on bedside examination (Hoover sign for functional leg weakness, tremor entrainment / distractibility for functional tremor, give-way weakness, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline splitting). Diagnosis of FND is made by these positive signs, not by exclusion alone.
optimal_actions.expected_finding: At least one reliable positive functional sign documented

useless_tools.rationale: ECG has no diagnostic role in FND; cardiac etiology is not on the differential for the presenting neurological deficit.
Echocardiography has no role in FND; no structural cardiac question is raised by the presentation.
Cardiac rhythm monitoring is not indicated; the events are non-syncopal and the rule-in signs point to FND.
Non-contrast head CT adds no information beyond MRI for an FND workup and contributes diagnostic noise plus radiation exposure.
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in typical FND; invasive testing reinforces somatic illness model and adds iatrogenic risk without changing management.
Advanced PET imaging has no indication in FND; standard MRI is the appropriate structural workup.

critical_actions: Document at least one positive rule-in sign (Hoover sign, tremor entrainment, distractibility, give-way pattern, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split)
Obtain brain MRI to exclude structural pathology
Obtain video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG to confirm PNES
Communicate the diagnosis transparently using positive language and the rule-in signs as the basis
Refer for FND-informed physiotherapy and CBT / psychological therapy
Order a comprehensive neuropsychological battery to characterize comorbid depression, anxiety, somatization, and trauma exposure — informs treatment planning (criteria-pack 'recommended' tier)
contraindicated_actions: Do not pursue ever-expanding negative investigations — per Stone 2018, repeated negative workups reinforce illness conviction and worsen prognosis
Do not frame the diagnosis as 'all in your head', 'nothing wrong', or 'we couldn't find anything' — this damages the therapeutic alliance and is the most common avoidable harm in FND
Do not perform invasive testing (lumbar puncture, nerve biopsy, muscle biopsy, cerebral angiography) when positive rule-in signs are present and there is no clinical indication
Do not order EMG/NCS, muscle biopsy, or nerve biopsy as part of an FND workup — these invasive tests reinforce the somatic illness model per Stone 2018
Do not start or continue long-term anti-epileptic drugs for functional (psychogenic non-epileptic) seizures — AEDs are ineffective for PNES and expose the patient to side effects
Do not give benzodiazepines as abortive therapy for witnessed PNES events (no benefit and risk of respiratory depression)
key_reasoning_points: FND is a positive diagnosis based on rule-in signs (Hoover, tremor entrainment, give-way weakness, non-dermatomal sensory loss with midline split) — not a diagnosis of exclusion (Espay 2018, Stone 2018).
Brain MRI and basic labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12) are due-diligence to exclude structural and reversible causes — they are NOT the route to the diagnosis, which is established at the bedside.
Over-investigation is the principal iatrogenic harm in FND; every additional negative test reinforces the patient's illness conviction and worsens prognosis (Stone 2018).
Psychiatric comorbidity (anxiety, depression, trauma) is common and informs treatment planning but is NOT required for the diagnosis and does not 'explain' the symptoms in a reductive sense.
Diagnostic communication matters: using positive language anchored on the rule-in signs is associated with better engagement and outcomes (Stone 2018).
Evidence-based treatment is multidisciplinary — CBT for PNES and FND-informed physiotherapy for functional motor symptoms (Nielsen 2015).
Video-EEG capturing a habitual event with normal interictal EEG is diagnostic for PNES (ILAE PNES Task Force 2013); routine EEG alone is insufficient.

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of multiple sclerosis in a relative
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on a demyelinating diagnosis (MS) and pursue extensive MS-specific workup before considering FND
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Non-first-degree family history of MS is a weak risk factor; the patient's symptoms must be evaluated on positive findings. Normal brain MRI without demyelinating lesions effectively addresses this concern.

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of epilepsy in a relative
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on an epileptic etiology and pursue prolonged AED trials before confirming PNES with video-EEG
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Family history of epilepsy does not establish the patient's events as epileptic. Video-EEG capturing the habitual event without ictal correlate is the gold standard.

red_herrings.data_point: Pre-existing psychiatric diagnosis (anxiety or depression) in the past medical history
red_herrings.intended_effect: Premature anchoring on a 'psychosomatic' label without obtaining positive rule-in signs; conversely, dismissing FND as a serious diagnosis because the patient is 'just anxious'
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Psychiatric comorbidity neither establishes nor refutes FND. Diagnosis requires positive rule-in signs on examination; psychiatric history is relevant for treatment planning, not for diagnosis.

red_herrings.data_point: Symptom onset coincident with a major psychosocial stressor
red_herrings.intended_effect: Conclude prematurely that stress 'caused' the symptoms and that the workup can be abbreviated
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Many organic conditions (MS, migraine, epilepsy) also flare with stress. Stress at onset is supportive context, not a diagnostic substitute for the positive rule-in signs.
